messages.subject: release of version 0.4 of NIMBLE, including many new features
messages.subject_clean: release of version 0.4 of NIMBLE, including many new features
messages.body_plain:
Dear nimble-users and nimble-announce,

We're pleased to announce that we've released version 0.4 of NIMBLE at
R-nimble.org.

Version 0.4 is a major release. Highlights include allowing users to define
their own functions and distributions for use in BUGS code and handling of
truncation, censoring, and general constraints in BUGS models. In addition,
we added functionality to the NIMBLE algorithm language.
Plus lots of back-end improvements that should result in faster model building,
configuration of MCMCs, and compilation of models and algorithms. More
details on the NIMBLE web page and the NEWS file of the package.

These are still early days for NIMBLE.  Please take a moment to let us
know what you're trying to use it for and what would make it better.
You can email the development team directly at nimble...@gmail.com
or share with the nimble-users list at nimble...@googlegroups.com.

 - Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team

Jose

messages.subject: Re: dsum JAGS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jose,

You can probably use our new (as of version 0.4) dconstraint functionality to mimic what dsum does. However, note (as also noted in the JAGS manual) that introducing an equality constraint can cause problems in MCMC sampling as a proposal would need to obey the constraints exactly.  So while you can probably introduce the constraint, I suspect you will not be able to fit the model.  You may be able to reparameterize your model to automatically obey the constraint and reduce the number of parameters by one.

messages.subject: Re: dsum JAGS
messages.body_plain:
Here is an example.  I want to echo what Chris said: I’m not sure this is the best path since representing constraints in different ways can lead to different results.  But for illustration here is an example:

## Example of adding a sampler that obeys a linear constraint
library(nimble)

## Make a model with two nodes, a and b.
## Suppose we want to sample with constraint a + b = c, where c will be data
## and we'll take care that we provide initial values that follow the constraint
sillyModel <- nimbleModel( nimbleCode({a ~ dnorm(0, 1); b ~ dnorm(0,1); c ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)}), inits = list(a = 0.3, b = 0.4), data = list(c = 0.7) )
## We don't really need a distribution for c.  It is just written as a way to get c as a node into the model.
## Maybe we should make a better way to do that.

## To do constrained sampling, we'll work temporarily in the space
## w1 = (a + b) ## i.e. w1 = c
## w2 = (a - b)
## Then we'll sample w2 as a random walk Metropolis-Hastings and convert back to a and b
RW_constrained <- nimbleFunction(
    contains = sampler_BASE,
    ## assume target is a vector of two nodes and control$constraint gives the constraint node
    setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
        scale = control$scale
        constraintNode <- control$constraintNode
        calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
    },
    run = function() {
        target_vals <- values(model, target)
        current_w2 <- target_vals[2] - target_vals[1] ## could use linear algebra for more general case
        current_w1 <- sum(target_vals)
        if(abs(model[[constraintNode]] - current_w1) > 1e-6) print('Looks like the constraint is being violated\n');
        proposal_w2 <- rnorm(1, current_w2, scale)
        target_vals[1] <- 0.5*(current_w1 - proposal_w2)
        target_vals[2] <- 0.5*(current_w1 + proposal_w2)
        values(model, target) <<- target_vals
        accept <- decide(calculateDiff(model, calcNodes))
        if(accept) {
            copy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
        } else {
            copy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)
        }
    },
    methods = list(
        reset = function() {}
    )
)

## Make an empty configuration by creating one and then removing the samplers
confMCMC <- configureMCMC(sillyModel)
confMCMC$getSamplers()
confMCMC$removeSamplers('a')
confMCMC$removeSamplers('b')
## alternatively we could do configureMCMC(sillyModel, nodes = NULL) to get an empty MCMC configuration directly (i.e. one with no samplers)

## now add one instance of our constrained sampler
confMCMC$addSampler(target = c('a','b'), type = RW_constrained, control = list(scale = 0.5, constraintNode = 'c'))

sillyMCMC <- buildMCMC(confMCMC)

cConstrainedExample <- compileNimble(sillyModel, sillyMCMC)

cConstrainedExample$sillyMCMC$run(10000)

samp <- as.matrix(cConstrainedExample$sillyMCMC$mvSamples)

plot(samp[,'a'])
plot(samp[,'b'])
plot(samp[,'a'], samp[, 'b'])
abline(0.7, -1, col = 'red') ## show the constraint

## end of example

Now one might want to use adaptive random walk instead of choosing a scale parameter as above.  To do that one could copy from samplers_RW in MCMC_samplers.R in the nimble/R directory of the source code.  One would then replace the first four lines of the run function with the first nine lines of the run function above.  (The error check could be removed).  A more general case of constraints could be done using linear algebra.

Perry

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: error building model
messages.body_plain:
Mathias sent me the code and I’m responding on the list so others can follow. (It’s published with this if you’re interested: Tobler, M.W., Zúñiga Hartley, A., Carrillo-Percastegui, S.E. & Powell, G.V.N. (2015) Spatiotemporal hierarchical modelling of species richness and occupancy using camera trap data. Journal of Applied Ecology, 52, 413-421.)

Turns out it was a simple issue to do with how NIMBLE treats “data” differently from JAGS and WinBUGS.  In NIMBLE “data” is a label for the role played by parts of a model, but the data values can be changed.  In NIMBLE “constants” are values that cannot be changed after model definition.

That means that vectors of indices must be provided as constants, not data. It only made sense for us to allow them as constants because they are used to determine the model structure (the graph).  If they were data, they could be changed, but that would change the structure of the model, which wouldn’t make sense.  It takes some getting used to when coming from JAGS or WinBUGS.

So Mathias, I was able to build the model simply by moving your three vectors of XXX.factor variables from your data list to your constants list.

A couple of other notes:

Posterior predictive nodes can be computed after the MCMC sampling, if you’d like.

For your model, the model checking step in nimbleModel() is slow, so I used “check = FALSE” in the call to nimbleModel.

For MCMC performance comparisons, a good idea is to compare effective sample size per time, rather than simply the system.time() for executing the MCMC.  You can use the effectiveSize() function from the coda package to get that.

Thanks and let us know other questions, comments or suggestions.

Perry

messages.subject: Re: error building model
messages.body_plain:
In case it's of interest to you, there's built-in functionality in NIMLBE to run and compare NIMBLE MCMC algorithms with those of JAGS, WinBUGS, OpenBUGS, and Stan (if you provide the Stan model specification).  It can also compare custom-defined NIMBLE MCMC algorithms, say, if you'd like to assign different samplers.  This is all done through NIMBLE's MCMCsuite.  ?MCMCsuite will explain the details of usage.  It provides a quick and easy way to do these comparisons, also optionally produce posterior density plots, traceplots, timing each algorithm, and optionally calculating effective sample sizes, custom posterior statistics, etc.

Let me know if this might be of interest to you, or if you try using the MCMCsuite and have any troubles.

Bigger picture, I'm glad your model is up and running in NIMBLE.

Cheers,
Daniel
